017d3ecc-7621-534c-a446-8ff49e50e583.title: Calligraphing the Sacred
017d3ecc-7621-534c-a446-8ff49e50e583.quote: These are eight calligraphic variations of the invocation formula Basmala “In the name of God, most Gracious, most Merciful”. The Quran begins the al-Fatiha Surah with this formula. The Basmala is one of the most frequently calligraphed sayings in the Arabic calligraphic tradition.

2a2c0daa-4c6a-509a-bda8-8d14fc7fd851.title: Symbiosis III
2a2c0daa-4c6a-509a-bda8-8d14fc7fd851.quote: Only a few of Haji Noor Deen’s works are constructed with a synopsis of the two writing systems. In an interview, he describes how difficult it is to find words that are appropriate for this type of calligraphy. For the artist, this requires several months and thought to design the piece to seamlessly combine both letterings systems together.

305c1d8e-112c-5d15-83c6-e4bfbf3d348e.title: Influences of Chinese Calligraphy
305c1d8e-112c-5d15-83c6-e4bfbf3d348e.quote: Chinese calligraphy, esteemed throughout East Asia, evolved from utility to abstract expression. It's seen as a window to the soul, merging with poetry and painting in the “three perfections”. This synergy captures reality through the artist's emotional resonance, achieved through rhythm, flow, and balance.

307e2c0b-7541-540b-8098-779634923cdc.title: The Two Traditions
307e2c0b-7541-540b-8098-779634923cdc.presentation:
In his work, Haji Noor Deen experiments with aspects of Arabic and Chinese calligraphy and explores their boundaries. Some of his works are more closely related to the Arabic writing tradition and others to the Chinese.  
  
The artist produces scrolls of colored silk onto which the calligraphy is mounted. The writing usually runs from top to bottom, however, on occasion he also uses a horizontal approach.  
  
What all of his works have in common is their religious content, which reflects the artist's deep faith.

326ddb0c-d7a1-53f5-bcaa-8516c0c93859.title: Haji Noor Deen and His Calligraphies
326ddb0c-d7a1-53f5-bcaa-8516c0c93859.presentation:
Born in Shandong Province, China, Haji Noor Deen perfected his craft over multiple decades. After studying Chinese calligraphy, he became inspired by the Arabic tradition and moved to Egypt where he embarked on a rigorous training programme, becoming the first Chinese artist in Egypt to receive the Master Arabic Calligraphy Certificate in 1997. As a demonstration of his aptitude, he earned the arduous Ijazah Certificate in 2017, unique in that it continues to uphold a traditional Ottoman approach to calligraphy practice in Turkey today. Haji Noor Deen harnesses his practice of both the Chinese and Arabic writing traditions and bridges their aesthetic principles with expressive brushstrokes.  
  
The artist’s unique calligraphy tools further reflect his synthesis of the two practices. He both employs the traditional pen (*qalam*) and the Chinese brush and even fashions new tools, such as wooden spatulas covered with fabric, to better negotiate the demands of disparate traditions.

39d3011d-76b8-59a2-9889-3c98a526967c.title: About
39d3011d-76b8-59a2-9889-3c98a526967c.presentation:
Sini calligraphy is the artistic script that has been used by the Muslim minority in China for centuries, with its history stretching back to the 14th century. The distinctive feature of Sini calligraphy is the melding of techniques and styles from the Arabic and Chinese lettering traditions.  
  
Haji Noor Deen is a master of Sini calligraphy. Inspired by calligraphic traditions spanning from China to Istanbul, the artist creates works with expressive lines that at first glance appear Chinese, but upon closer inspection go far beyond that.

3cca71b6-8430-5074-87d7-d7fc23a6441e.title: Influences of Arabic Calligraphy
3cca71b6-8430-5074-87d7-d7fc23a6441e.quote: Classical Arabic calligraphy entails rigorous rules, honed since the 10th century, demanding years of practice. Haji Noor Deen, a trained calligrapher, adeptly blends tradition with innovation, prioritizing harmony over strict adherence, transcending classical norms for a holistic artistic expression.

48cdda94-75f8-517d-875e-082064d5ec30.title: Variations of the Basmala
48cdda94-75f8-517d-875e-082064d5ec30.presentation:
The Quran begins the al-Fatiha surah with the invocation phrase *Basmala,* “In the name of God, most Gracious, most Merciful”. The Basmala is one of the most frequently calligraphed sayings in the Arabic calligraphic tradition.  
  
For Haji Noor Deen, the Basmala is to be understood as the essence of the Quran, and explains why he has been continually developing new variations of writing it for over 40 years. So far, he has succeeded in realising over 300 different compositions and ways of writing it.  
  
The variations compiled here deal with plants and nature. Some of the flower paintings are executed in the tradition of Chinese painting. The artists perceives the preoccupation with nature as a symbol of hope and inexhaustible life. At the same time, he wishes to impart advice to us all, that life and nature are valued and that we should not treat this wealth wastefully and destructively: “Our planet Earth is a common home on which humanity depends. All people should shape the earth in harmony with nature”.

63f893e2-4d29-5a06-9725-39a71cf2389c.title: Islam in China
63f893e2-4d29-5a06-9725-39a71cf2389c.presentation:
More than 25 million Muslims live in China today. The largest communities include the Turkic Uyghurs in the region of Xinjiang and the Chinese-speaking Hui Muslims, scattered throughout the country’s provinces.  
  
Political and economic connections between China and West Asia stretch back to antiquity. After the spread of Islam, Arab traders travelled to Tang Dynasty China (AD 618–907) and became the first Muslims to live in China. Following the Mongol conquests, the Yuan Dynasty (AD 1271–1368) retained strong ties to Central and West Asia, and exchange across the entire Asian continent increased exponentially.  
  
The rise of the Ming dynasty (AD 1368–1644), ruled by Han Chinese, brought great changes for the Muslims in China. From then on, they were a religious minority called Hui Muslims. Over the centuries, this led to the gradual integration of Islam into Chinese traditions and culture. Evidence of their art manifests itself in Sini calligraphy, with inscriptions on wood, stone, and metal, as well as being present in book art and characteristic mosque architecture.

7854ada7-a8f9-53bf-a243-8dd5b2277f24.title: Hui Muslims
7854ada7-a8f9-53bf-a243-8dd5b2277f24.quote: The rise of the Ming Dynasty (AD 1368–1644), ruled by the Han Chinese, brought great changes for the Muslims in China. From then on, they were a religious minority called Hui Muslims. Over the centuries, this led to the gradual integration of Islam into Chinese traditions and culture. Evidence of their art is found in Sini calligraphy (with inscriptions on wood, stone and metal), book art, and characteristic mosque architecture.

7aa652f9-3d7a-5950-ae09-62acd79f2cba.title: Calligraphy Tools
7aa652f9-3d7a-5950-ae09-62acd79f2cba.quote: The artist's tools span various cultures: Chinese calligraphy uses brushes, Arabic calligraphy employs qalams. Haji Noor Deen combines both, using spatulas of varied materials. Traditional Chinese ink, seals, red seal paste, and metal weights are also integral to his process.

ab0ea891-6907-5c56-bf8c-bda2a6378a90.title: Chinese Characters
ab0ea891-6907-5c56-bf8c-bda2a6378a90.quote: Chinese writing, among the world's oldest, utilises characters representing morphemes, the smallest units of meaning. Each character often denotes a syllable or word, intertwining sound and meaning. Haji Noor Deen ingeniously merges Arabic with Chinese components in calligraphy, as seen in “Peace”.

aecff04f-7897-545e-919c-e5f7a5f6651e.title: Symbiosis II
aecff04f-7897-545e-919c-e5f7a5f6651e.quote: This calligraphy also manages to achive a complete symbiosis between Arabic and Chinese. According to Haji Noor Deen, it is very complicated to construct calligraphies with both writing systems.

c4623145-c923-5a92-840e-59a70f5c5044.title: Seals
c4623145-c923-5a92-840e-59a70f5c5044.quote: Seals, integral to Chinese calligraphy, serve as artistic signatures, ensuring authenticity. Haji Noor Deen creatively combines Arabic and Chinese in his seals, emphasizing balanced composition. Traditionally, square seals go on the left, while oval seals, often containing sayings, are placed on the top right.

d0d91b52-4de7-5a36-8160-5f3eaaf261b4.title: Haji Noor Deen and His Scripts
d0d91b52-4de7-5a36-8160-5f3eaaf261b4.quote: Haji Noor Deen expertly mimics various Chinese scripts in his calligraphy, such as cursive or seal script, ingeniously blending them with Arabic. In works like “The Beautiful Names of God” and “I Take Refuge with God”, he seamlessly integrates Arabic into Chinese-style scripts. By merging two distinct calligraphic traditions and languages to repeatedly craft innovative styles, he showcases his mastery and creativity in Sini script.

d730136a-6126-5248-9219-65c05233157b.title: Symbiosis I
d730136a-6126-5248-9219-65c05233157b.quote: Three works display a fusion of Arabic and Chinese calligraphy. All three can be read in both Chinese and Arabic.

e35e5041-aa99-5b57-93cb-323e3b124b7c.title: Chinese-Arabic Calligraphy
e35e5041-aa99-5b57-93cb-323e3b124b7c.presentation:
Calligraphy is the most revered art form in Islamic cultures due to its relationship to the Qur’an. Its practitioners are able to achieve exquisite accuracy using the Qalam, the classical writing tool made of reeds. Over the centuries, various types of writing have developed which precisely specify proportions and lengths within the script.  
  
Chinese-Arabic calligraphy originated in China in the 13th to 14th centuries and is a synthesis of Arabic and Chinese writing traditions. Known as "Sini calligraphy" from the Arabic word for China (*al-Sin*), it is still today practiced by Chinese Hui Muslims.  
  
Characteristic of Sini calligraphy are curved, broad letters written with a brush rather than a pen. Compared to classical Arabic calligraphy, Sini calligraphy is completely free of guidelines. Instead, the highest commandment is the perceived beauty and the balance of the composition. The direction of writing can be freely chosen, either from top to bottom, as in Chinese, or from right to left, as in Arabic. The texts can also be either Chinese or Arabic and usually have religious content.

7aa652f9-3d7a-5950-ae09-62acd79f2cba/ec2.contextual_description: Here we can see the tools used by Haji Noor Deen for his works on rice paper.

c4623145-c923-5a92-840e-59a70f5c5044/63a.contextual_description: Oval seals used by Haji Noor Deen

c4623145-c923-5a92-840e-59a70f5c5044/bc3.contextual_description: Square seals used by Haji Noor Deen

d730136a-6126-5248-9219-65c05233157b/377.contextual_description: With strong, broad brushstrokes, Haji Noor Deen forms this calligraphy, which gives rise to the word “God” in both Chinese and Arabic. The letters seem to form a stylised figure that humbly bows its head. Thus, the physical symbiosis of the Arabic and Chinese writing systems is complemented by a figurative one.

d730136a-6126-5248-9219-65c05233157b/951.contextual_description: The graphic shows the course of the Arabic letters, which can be read turned to the left.

aecff04f-7897-545e-919c-e5f7a5f6651e/32e.contextual_description: This calligraphy shows the Chinese word *Sheng* (Prophet), which at the same time can be read as *Rasul Allah* (Messenger of God) in Arabic.

aecff04f-7897-545e-919c-e5f7a5f6651e/569.contextual_description: The graphic shows the course of the Arabic letters, which can be read turned to the left.

2a2c0daa-4c6a-509a-bda8-8d14fc7fd851/75d.contextual_description: The Muslim profession of faith (Shahada) reads: “There is no God but God and Muhammad is his messenger”. Haji Noor Deen chooses a complex calligraphy that, amazingly, works in both Chinese and Arabic scripts. A demonstration of the artist’s unique ability to create a true symbiosis of the writing systems.

2a2c0daa-4c6a-509a-bda8-8d14fc7fd851/8a2.contextual_description: The graphic shows the course of the Arabic letters, which can be read turned to the left.

3cca71b6-8430-5074-87d7-d7fc23a6441e/389.contextual_description: Densely arranged, the multiline calligraphy forms the shape of a leaf. Three quotations from the Qur’an come together here: “God is the light of heavens and earth” (sura 24, verse 35), “I trust in God” (sura 11, verse 56), and “In the remembrance of God, do hearts find rest” (sura 13, verse 28).

3cca71b6-8430-5074-87d7-d7fc23a6441e/63d.contextual_description: Here, too, the *Shahada*, the Muslim profession of faith, is calligraphed, but the composition is quite different from those seen before. Haji Noor Deen works intensively with script formats and variations of writing. The work here is entirely in the tradition of Arabic calligraphy, in which images are sometimes formed from letters.

3cca71b6-8430-5074-87d7-d7fc23a6441e/041.contextual_description: The eulogy *Subhan Allah* (God is sublime) is used in daily speech in the context of a positive event. Haji Noor Deen creates an expressive and well-balanced composition.

305c1d8e-112c-5d15-83c6-e4bfbf3d348e/a33.contextual_description: Calligraphic variation of the invocation formula Basmala, “In the name of God, most Gracious, most Merciful”. Despite having Islamic connotations, the piece deals with plants and nature, and uses Chinese stylisation and techniques to depict some of the flowers in order to create this hybrid piece. The artist sees in the occupation with nature a symbol of hope and inexhaustible life.

305c1d8e-112c-5d15-83c6-e4bfbf3d348e/f39.contextual_description: In this display, there are two variations of the proclamation of faith. Here, the letters of the *Shahada* (“There is no God but God and Muhammad is his prophet”) form a flower in a symmetrical composition. It alludes to God as the creator of nature.

305c1d8e-112c-5d15-83c6-e4bfbf3d348e/49a.contextual_description: Calligraphic variation of the invocation formula Basmala “In the name of God, most Gracious, most Merciful”. The artist wants to advise that life and nature be valued and that we do not treat this wealth wastefully and destructively: “Our planet Earth is a common home on which humanity depends. All people should shape the earth in harmony with nature.”

305c1d8e-112c-5d15-83c6-e4bfbf3d348e/f50.contextual_description: In this calligraphy, the proclamation of faith forms a flower. Individual letters are difficult to recognise; they are strongly abstracted.

ab0ea891-6907-5c56-bf8c-bda2a6378a90/92d.contextual_description: The artist impressively composes the word *al-Salam* (peace) by repeatedly writing the Muslim profession of faith (*Shahada*), with the first part (“There is no God but God”) as an outline and the second part (“and Muhammad is his prophet”) filling in the letters.

d0d91b52-4de7-5a36-8160-5f3eaaf261b4/4c1.contextual_description: This calligraphy is dedicated to the most beautiful names of God as they appear in the Qur’an. In the two central medallions are God (right) and Muhammad (left). The script is Arabic, even though the form and composition are Chinese. The text is written in columns from top to bottom and from right to left and has a well-balanced composition.

d0d91b52-4de7-5a36-8160-5f3eaaf261b4/a46.contextual_description: On this scroll, Haji Noor Deen creates a calligraphy that looks Chinese at first glance. On closer inspection, however, it turns out that the text is written in Arabic characters. Starting with the *Isti’adhah*, the seeking for refuge and shelter he continues with a quote from the second verse of the Qur’an (2:255).

7854ada7-a8f9-53bf-a243-8dd5b2277f24/a82.contextual_description: This plate from the late 15th century is a good example of Sini calligraphy applied on Chinese porcelain. The decoration combines Arabic calligraphy with Chinese ornaments and designs.

7854ada7-a8f9-53bf-a243-8dd5b2277f24/0f8.contextual_description: This censer from the 17th century might have been used in a mosque. The Arabic calligraphy once again shows the Muslim declaration of faith.

7854ada7-a8f9-53bf-a243-8dd5b2277f24/a47.contextual_description: This Qur’an from the 17th to 18th century is written in classic Arabic naskh calligraphy, but the decorations follow the Chinese ornament tradition. The manuscript is written on rice paper, which is also typical of Sini calligraphy.
